title: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite range of small measures
description: This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is p
body: This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published, external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address – but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value – and others that some will likely curse.There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT – the big revenue generators – they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary. That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.The central challenge for Healey, which he shares with his recent predecessors, is the public finances are in a mess and so are the personal finances of so, so many households. And there is a recurring sense of déjà vu in the language of the OBR. "The UK's economic and fiscal position remains very challenging," it says, with a splash of understatement, adding that "there have been further adverse developments" this year with in the conflict in the Middle East.As for what happens, next, well, frankly, who on earth knows. Or, as the OBR puts it: "The outlook for the economy and the public finances is uncertain, with significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability."The Budget book argues that "the UK economy is showing signs of resilience" but it is also true that the national debt, tax burden, inflation and interest rates are high, going up or both – and there could yet be further economic shocks that make things worse.What happens, for instance, in the Middle East, once the mid term elections are done in America and the result of the Israeli general election is clear?In short, the chancellor felt constrained in his capacity to act and his capacity to make a noticeable positive difference is perhaps constrained even more so – because any intervention, even expensive ones, may merely make a grim situation a bit less bad, rather than things actually feeling better. Mitigating the bad is arguably a noble political aim, but it costs money and potentially comes with little political upside.Instead there is this fleet of smaller measures that the government will hope gives their MPs something to try to sell – while acknowledging that they are not world changing.Luke Tryl, the UK Director of the More in Common think tank, says: "The softly populist tone of this budget is likely to land well with the public. The Chancellor targeted groups the public have little sympathy with - banks, landlords, gambling companies and vape shops - and turned it into cost-of-living support, rate relief for small businesses and ensuring the state pension isn't taxed."He adds: "Crucially, the chancellor may have avoided the biggest potential trap of the Budget - being seen to offer energy support for those on benefits and incurring the ire of the squeezed middle, who think they work hard but are left to fend for themselves. "Instead, by offering support to all of those on Council Tax bands A to D, he is able to reassure them that the government will support them too."The reaction of the opposition parties, from a range of different political perspectives, amounts to a critique that this Budget was thin. The government counters that it is one piece in the emerging jigsaw of detail from the new-ish prime minister and his chancellor – with a plan help young people into work and cut benefits before Christmas, alongside a big picture sense of what the UK's long term relationship with the European Union could look like and a 10 year vision from Andy Burnham.In summary, this felt like a cautious Budget. One critical friend of the government suggested to me this would be a "Mr Sensible Budget" – their hope and expectation that it might be shorn of bells and whistles, but shorn of timebombs too. Let's see.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite range of small measures

title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 21 minutes agoUp to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to he
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 21 minutes agoUp to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.Here's what you need to know about the payment.How much is it?For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.A typical yearly energy bill is forecast to jump by £276 in January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight, so many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.However, some more recent forecasts suggest a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January. If so, the saving would be only a quarter of that.Will I get the payment? And how can I check?Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.Will I get it if I live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland?The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.He urged the devolved governments to follow suit to "give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter".The Welsh government has said that it will also make a £100 cost-of-living payment to all households in council tax bands A to D.The Scottish government said it would "seek to replicate" the £100 energy payment.How do I get the money? Will I get it if I'm a student or don't pay council tax?If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.Do I have to spend the money on my energy bill?The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts. As such, people could choose to spend it on something else.How is the government funding this payment?The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

title: John Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
description: Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defen
body: Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag. The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding:  "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending". He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets. Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending.Earlier this year, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped in order to pay for increased defence spending. Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%. "He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said. The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security". Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030. Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030. "And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".The chancellor said this would include:starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resources increasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnershipsdirecting the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put £5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn. Helen Millier, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities."There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees. The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility. A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency. Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow". He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

title: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered
description: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.It was abundan
body: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes. Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament, a sign of how much the war has blown prosperity off course.But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out. And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

schema.headline: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered

title: How could Israel break political deadlock? Here are four scenarios
description: Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed him
body: Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority. The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside. However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.

schema.headline: How could Israel break political deadlock? Here are four scenarios

title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
description: Figure caption, Israel's election result is messy - here's whyByDavid GrittenPartial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Ministe
body: Figure caption, Israel's election result is messy - here's whyByDavid GrittenPartial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers and diplomats yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades."It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction."We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.Image source, EPAImage caption, Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc."The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority"."We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."The leader of the left-wing Democrats party told its partners in Eisenkot's bloc on Wednesday that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition."We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," Yair Golan wrote on X.The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - appear to be heading for record representation because of a strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.The chairman of the Joint List, which has talked of providing an electoral "safety net" for the Jewish opposition, said on Wednesday that it was "ready and prepared to pave the way to oust the Netanyahu government"."Change runs through a Jewish-Arab partnership - a genuine and equal partnership. Nothing less, and nothing more," Yousef Jabareen wrote on X.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hardline, religious-nationalist trajectory.Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

title: Manchester United: Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes hold clear-the-air talks
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have held clear-the-air talks before the team's trip to Chelsea.Fernandes, 32
body: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have held clear-the-air talks before the team's trip to Chelsea.Fernandes, 32, was an unused substitute during United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth on Sunday.The Portuguese was dropped to the bench after he criticised Carrick's tactics following the 4-1 loss against Como in the Champions League.Sources have told BBC Sport that the pair spoke privately at the club's training ground on Tuesday, with the talks aimed at airing issues.It is unclear whether Fernandes, who was made club captain in 2023, apologised for his critical comments.United are preparing for Saturday's trip to Chelsea (12:30 GMT), when Fernandes could return to the starting line-up.Carrick was widely expected to be sacked following the Bournemouth game, but he will take charge of the Premier League match at Stamford Bridge.United's board decided the 45-year-old deserved the opportunity to turn things around at Old Trafford, despite the team languishing in 16th place in the Premier League.There was further good news for Carrick on Wednesday, with midfielder Kobbie Mainoo returning to training after a fortnight out through injury.Despite managing just one victory in eight Premier League matches this term, the predicament at the club is not seen as being entirely Carrick's fault by the board.Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some blame.One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone."Nevertheless, sources have told BBC Sport that the club have shortlisted former Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany and Bayern Munich head coach Julian Nagelsmann as potential replacements for Carrick.Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million-pound compensation claim from his former club Newcastle, while Nagelsmann is a free agent.

schema.headline: Manchester United: Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes hold clear-the-air talks

title: Four investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress
description: Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investiga
body: Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations."We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC.Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities -  particularly cryptocurrency firms -  as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family."What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said.The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing."President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said."Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added.A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress.Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position."[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats."Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny."The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said. "The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions.In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters"."By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department.Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time.Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences.Others have called for a more cautious approach, arguing that any impeachment is unlikely to end in the Senate voting to remove Trump - who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing - from office.It is also unclear whether the party could agree on a reason to launch impeachment proceedings."I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office in October, adding that he sees the impeachment efforts in his first term and the later criminal cases brought against him as "very illegal things".James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the Washington Sun news outlet in June that Democrats were "one-trick ponies" who were "going to go after Trump".There is no guarantee for Democrats that any potential investigation would end with a meaningful outcome.But Subramanyam said their efforts would send a message."If we do not do something because we are scared of the optics, or we don't think it will be successful, or they stonewall us, that will be bad," he said. "Not just for the next two years, but for the next 20 years."

schema.headline: Four investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress

title: Thierry Henry responds to backlash over Ballon d'Or comments
description: Thierry Henry has defended himself after criticism over the way he hosted Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony.The former France and Arsenal forward, who has
body: Thierry Henry has defended himself after criticism over the way he hosted Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony.The former France and Arsenal forward, who has come under fire for remarks he made towards Barcelona star Lamine Yamal, overall winner Harry Kane and co-host Kate Scott on the night, has addressed what he said was "people getting really excited about nothing".Henry, who was presenting the ceremony alongside CBS Sports colleague Scott, joked with Lamine Yamal about him winning a third successive young player of the year award.He also corrected Scott's pronunciation of Brazil legend Socrates' name and admitted he wanted fellow Frenchman Kylian Mbappe to beat Kane to the top prize.Addressing the Lamine Yamal situation, which received an audible reaction from the audience in attendance, Henry said he wasn't "checking his ego" and emphasised his admiration of the young Spaniard.On the night, he teased Lamine Yamal by saying of his young player award: "It's your third one, right? But is it the one you really wanted to win?"Speaking in a social media video on Wednesday, Henry said: "I'm a big fan of Lamine Yamal. I wasn't checking his ego at all - that you didn't like the joke, I can understand."But don't do that, he's one of the players I'd pay to watch, I love him."The 49-year-old also responded to criticism over his response to co-host Scott's pronunciation of 'Socrates', claiming she was in on the joke herself."You didn't like the joke, I understand, but please stop saying I disrespected Kate," Henry said."I will never do that and you can ask her, she was on the joke with me. She did Soc on purpose, and I said Soc, so please stop inventing stories."Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka won the Socrates Award for his humanitarian and charity work.Henry added Kane was a "worthy winner" of the Ballon d'Or before telling everyone to "relax" after his support of Mbappe's claim to the prize."I'm French and I was always going to back up and support my fellow countryman," he said."I said to [Kane], 'You are a worthy winner, you deserve it, you are the example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is a talent'. Well done, Harry Kane - and I call him Sir Harry Kane since the World Cup."So please, people out there, relax, relax. I love Harry Kane, I love Lamine Yamal and I didn't disrespect Kate. She was on the joke with me."

schema.headline: Thierry Henry responds to backlash over Ballon d'Or comments

title: Arsenal to appeal against Max Dowman's red card against Fleetwood in Carabao Cup
description: Arsenal will appeal against Max Dowman's sending-off during Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie at Fleetwood.The 16-year-old midfielder was shown a straight red
body: Arsenal will appeal against Max Dowman's sending-off during Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie at Fleetwood.The 16-year-old midfielder was shown a straight red card in the 85th minute after reacting to a heavy challenge by Fleetwood's Harrison Neal.Although Dowman did not fully kick out, his foot did make contact with Neal.The game finished 1-1 before League Two Fleetwood beat the Premier League champions 5-3 on penalties.It was Dowman's second red card this month having also been sent off while representing England's Under-19s.As Dowman left the field, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and made what appeared to be an angry comment to the young winger.Arteta said after the game: "When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear."Dowman was dismissed for violent conduct, which according to the laws of the game is when a player "uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball... regardless of whether contact is made".As it stands, Dowman will face a three-match suspension.The Gunners were already light on options on the wing as Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke are currently out injured.Arteta's side return to Premier League action away to Liverpool on Sunday.

schema.headline: Arsenal to appeal against Max Dowman's red card against Fleetwood in Carabao Cup

title: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies aged 96
description: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.Huerta campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chave
body: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.Huerta campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chavez for farm workers' rights in the 1960s and 1970s, founding the United Farm Workers Union (UFW) with him.Through her foundation, Huerta had continued her activism work addressing immigration and voting issues. "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," family spokesman Erik Olvera said on Wednesday. Born in New Mexico, Huerta grew up in Stockton, California, in the heart of the state's large agricultural industry. She was raised by her mother, who at one point worked at a cannery. Huerta first became a teacher after graduating from university, before turning to organising workers. She later worked on civil and women's rights, as well as environmental issues, all while raising 11 children."I would like to be remembered as a woman who cares for fellow humans," she is reported by multiple sources to have once said. "We must use our lives to make the world a better place to live, not just to acquire things. That is what we are put on the earth for."Earlier this year, Huerta said Chavez, who died in 1993, had "manipulated and pressured" her into having sex and on another occasion forced her in the 1960s.That was after the New York Times published an investigation detailing allegations from Huerta and two other women, who said Chavez groomed and sexually abused girls involved in the labour movement.Huerta said the two encounters with Chavez resulted in pregnancies that she chose to keep secret, arranging for the children to be raised by other families.Chavez's family said in a statement at the time that they were "devastated" by the reports and praised the women's "courage to come forward".The UFW was among those paying tribute to Huerta, who reportedly died of cancer, on Wednesday, saying in a statement posted to social media that she had coined its motto - "Si Se Puede!", Spanish for "Yes, we can!" - which became a familiar rallying cry for activists seeking better working conditions for Hispanic farm workers. "Her life's work was to empower her community to face and overcome injustices, and she has left farm workers and the entire Latino community stronger and more organised than she found it," the UFW said. "Her commitment to civic engagement and bringing political power to disenfranchised people is a lesson we all should carry to the ballot box."Huerta also helped end what was known as the Bracero Program, where Mexican men were brought to work temporarily into the US, and helped negotiate the 1986 Immigration Reform Act, according to the union.The president of the voting group Voto Latino, María Teresa Kumar, called Huerta a "civil rights giant" who gave "her entire life, until her final days, to championing and fighting injustice for everyone, no matter who they were or where they came from". The Congressional Hispanic Caucus, made up of Democrats from the Senate and House of Representatives, said in a statement on Wednesday that "Dolores Huerta defied definition". "A national and international icon, her legacy is woven into the fabric of our history," they also said. "Her fight for justice will continue to inspire generations. Rest in power, hermana."

schema.headline: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies aged 96

title: Spanish rail crash: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster
description: Figure caption, Watch: 'People flew off their seats,' says passengerByPaulin KolaIt was approaching 09:00 (08:00 GMT) and two high-speed trains were t
body: Figure caption, Watch: 'People flew off their seats,' says passengerByPaulin KolaIt was approaching 09:00 (08:00 GMT) and two high-speed trains were travelling south from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville.One, run by state-owned operator Renfe had 397 passengers on board. Ahead of it on the same line was a train of Iryo private operator with 147 passengers. A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.Then the impossible happened, Spain's transport minister said, as the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error".It crashed into the back of the other train between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid.Broken arms, broken nosesSpanish journalist Roberto Gómez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train, when the train stopped and an announcement was relayed to passengers that there was congestion on the tracks. The train eventually began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened."The impact was terrible," he told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."Gómez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head."We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.In the last carriage of the Renfe train, Miguel Ángel Pérez observed a similar scene. "It was a terrible crash. The carriage partially overturned," he told Spanish TV program La Hora de La 1. "Luckily there were few people standing," he said. Passengers then jumped out of the carriage through the windows.The train that was hit from behind was one of six to have been ordered to halt at 08:30. It was still stationary when the order was given to the Renfe train to proceed.Transport Minister Óscar Puente appeared in front of the cameras to say an employee had ordered the resumption of travel at 08:36 and some 17 minutes later the "truly unbelievable" had happened. Sebastián Herrero from Seville was on the Iryo train and experienced the crash first hand.He felt a "terrible, terrible impact" and was thrown on to the seats in front of him, he told El Mundo newspaper."After we fell, there were many people with broken noses, broken arms... We started seeing smoke everywhere."Another man, who was not identified, told Reuters news agency: "Everything was overturned. Some people were thrown into the air. They are very badly injured."Image source, EPAImage caption, The crash near Urda is Spain's worst rail disaster since 2013Eduarda was also on the stationary train, travelling with her two cats.She told Cadena Ser radio how the crash had propelled her forwards.Once outside, the chaos hit her. She heard screams and saw people under the train who she said had died, and a carriage was on fire. For Fernando Seco the worst came after he left the train and saw a "horrible scene"."There were many injured people, a lot of blood and many dead," he said.How could this happen?Some of the fortunate passengers who escaped injury in the crash began helping others. Even injured and bloodied passengers did their best to help.It was not long before local people arrived, followed by the police and ambulance services of the Guardia Civil."People from neighbouring towns brought water," a volunteer told Reuters. "We are distributing it, especially to be taken to the accident site where people are in worse condition." Some residents brought cars to help with the evacuation to the nearby town of Urda, he explained.Spain was already reeling from the Adamuz high-speed rail disaster outside Córdoba in January, in which 46 people died.It happened on the same high-speed rail line, but much further south. So Wednesday's accident has raised many questions for the authorities. The Spanish transport minister said the circumstances were "inexplicable".According to regulations, under such circumstances, a train driver would be required to proceed at what is known as "sight speed" - about 40km/h (25mph), a speed that allows them to stop in time if they encounter an obstacle. Officials will investigate what order the Renfe train got, if it was travelling at the usual speed for that section of track - "around 200km/h" according to the minister, and, more significantly, why did the operator not stop its journey when his screen would have displayed that another train on the same line was stationary.Affected passengers were visibly angry."It isn't possible that our train was stopped for five or 10 minutes and that the other train wasn't told to stop," one of them said."How can this happen with the technology we have?," he added. "It's not normal. We weren't told anything. The person who should have been told something was the driver of the other train. We wouldn't have cared as long as the other train had been warned. I don't understand this."

schema.headline: Spanish rail crash: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster

title: Workers should be able to know colleagues' salaries, rights body says
description: Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.Bosses should be required to respo
body: Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed, external.In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said.Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.The EHRC urged lawmakers to make it compulsory for employers to provide information including colleagues' basic pay and hours worked, how employees' pay compares with each other, and information about bonuses, overtime, shift-premiums and performance-related pay, within a specific timeframe.The rights watchdog argued that this would help cut pay discrimination, especially against women.Women would also benefit from employers publishing salary details in job adverts, the EHRC has said previously, external.

schema.headline: Workers should be able to know colleagues' salaries, rights body says

title: Londonderry: Viable explosive device sent to hotel in package
description: Police believe dissident republicans may be responsible for a "viable postal device" which was delivered to a hotel in Londonderry.Ammunition Technica
body: Police believe dissident republicans may be responsible for a "viable postal device" which was delivered to a hotel in Londonderry.Ammunition Technical Officers (ATO) were tasked to the hotel at Ebrington Square in the Waterside after the package was discovered at about 15:20 GMT on Tuesday.They carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later taken away for a forensic examination.Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Supt Gillian Kearney condemned it as "shameful and utterly abhorrent", adding that "those responsible clearly do not care who or what they harm"."We are keeping an open mind as to who is responsible, and we are working through a number of lines of enquiry, one of which, at this time, is that dissident republicans may be responsible," Kearney said.She said the investigation was at an early stage and has appealed to anyone with information to come forward as "it could make all the difference".Ulster Unionist councillor Darren Guy, who chairs the local policing and community safety partnership, believes the incident was timed to cause maximum disruption.He also said it may have been linked to the MoD being represented at a careers event at the hotel in September."Recently, there was a careers event held in that hotel where I believe an RAF [Royal Air Force] stall was there for the careers event at that time."This was specifically done this week to cause as much disruption as possible during the 40th Halloween celebrations with thousands of international visitors visiting the city and the amount of families, especially young families going out to enjoy the many things on offer. "It is totally reckless and these people don't think about anyone else but themselves."Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson said it was too early to "speculate" about any link between the alert and the jobs fair."We need clarification from those responsible," Jackson said.He said this was "a disgusting attack on the city and the people of Derry". "There is no justification whatsoever for carrying this out and putting people in danger, especially when the city is gearing up for the 40th anniversary of the Halloween festival," he added."Derry is a warm and welcoming place and it's disgusting why someone or some organisation did this."Foyle SDLP MP Colum Eastwood told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme the incident must have been terrifying for those members of the public in the vicinity of the hotel ."This was clearly a viable device which is really frightening for the staff and the visitors to the hotel and to the hundreds, probably thousands of kids who were at that funfair yesterday and have been over the past number of days," Eastwood said."I don't know what entered someone's head to think this was a good idea."It is appalling, reckless and achieves absolutely nothing."Julie Middleton, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member for Foyle, told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme on Wednesday that she was "deeply disturbed and disgusted"."There is no excuse to leave a viable device anywhere at all, but in the middle of Ebrington Square, where you have people at their work, families out enjoying some half-term fun and tourists visiting and unfortunately this was designed to cause disruption and with any viable device, it was obviously designed to cause harm," she said.

schema.headline: Londonderry: Viable explosive device sent to hotel in package
